title: Moiré-induced lattice reconstruction at buried atomic interfaces
authors: Nicholas Clark, Frederick Allars, Isaac Soltero, Wendong Wang, David Hopkinson, Hugo de Latour, James G. McHugh, William Talbott, Sam Sullivan-Allsop, Rongsheng Cai, Astrid Weston, Xiao Li, Gareth Tainton, Casey K. Cheung, Francisco Selles, Alex Summerfield, Andrey Kretinin, Christopher S. Allen, Vladimir Falko, Sarah J. Haigh, Roman Gorbachev
abstract: Atomic reconstruction at twisted two-dimensional interfaces governs many of their emergent optical, electronic, and mechanical properties, including sliding ferroelectricity. Despite recent progress in understanding lattice reconstruction in suspended twisted bilayers, structural changes at van der Waals heterointerfaces between multilayer crystals remain largely unexplored. Here we use multi-slice electron ptychography to non-invasively recover the three-dimensional atomic structure at marginally twisted rhombohedral interfaces between thick transition-metal dichalcogenide crystals. With a position precision of ~3 pm and a depth resolution ~1 nm, we resolve the twist-induced lattice reconstruction field per layer, and the resulting dislocation network at the buried interface. Despite the bulk nature, we observe markedly strong in-plane interfacial reconstruction due to suppression of the out-of-plane bending by outer layers, exceeding predictions from our three-dimensional modelling. Furthermore, we extract the strain tensor evolution during the decay of the reconstruction into the bulk, providing a structural foundation for understanding multi-layer moiré systems.
summary: This work pioneers the use of multi-slice electron ptychography to map the 3D atomic structure at buried, twisted van der Waals interfaces in TMD crystals. Researchers observed significant, twist-induced lattice reconstruction at these interfaces, which was stronger than predicted by theory. By combining these high-resolution measurements with continuum modeling, the study provides a structural foundation for understanding the emergent electronic properties of moiré systems.
main_problem: The study investigates the structural changes, specifically lattice reconstruction, that occur at buried van der Waals heterointerfaces between multilayer crystals.
main_result: Strong, twist-induced in-plane lattice reconstruction was observed at the buried interface, exceeding theoretical predictions, and the technique allowed mapping the decay of this reconstruction into the bulk material.
method: The research combines advanced experimental techniques, namely multi-slice electron ptychography, with detailed theoretical modeling based on continuum mechanics and energy minimization.
model_or_system: The physical system involves marginally twisted rhombohedral interfaces between thick transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMD) crystals like $	ext{MoS}_2$. The theoretical model incorporates adhesion, in-plane elastic, and bending energies to predict layer-resolved atomic relaxation.
key_observables: Three-dimensional atomic structure, twist-induced lattice reconstruction field, dislocation network, strain tensor evolution, and root-mean-squared (rms) displacement decay.
important_parameters: Position precision of $\sim 3 	ext{ pm}$, depth resolution of $\sim 1 	ext{ nm}$, and twist angles ($	heta$) ranging from $0.2^\circ$ to $4^\circ$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the outer layers suppress out-of-plane bending, enhancing in-plane reconstruction, and that the reconstruction effect decays predictably away from the interface.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate depth-dependent atomic structures via ptychography, showing reconstructed domains ($	ext{MX}', 	ext{XM}'$) at the interface, and displacement maps showing the decay of reconstruction away from the buried junction.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the experimental capability using ptychography to image buried interfaces. It then presents the structural findings, detailing the observed reconstruction patterns and the decay profile of these distortions as a function of depth and twist angle. Finally, it compares these findings against continuum mechanical models.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state structure, the ability to map strain and structural phase transitions at interfaces using highly sensitive, non-invasive techniques is relevant to understanding emergent quantum properties in moiré heterostructures.
